3841.content:
A semi-supervised embedding maps data into a lower-dimensional space that preserves unsupervised geometry while drawing must-linked or same-labeled points together and separating incompatible ones. Clustering is then performed in the learned representation.

The balance between structural preservation and supervision determines whether the embedding generalizes beyond the guided examples. Excessive constraint weight can collapse local geometry into the few relationships that were labeled.

3844.content:
Semi-automatic reconstruction combines user-supplied constraints with computational fitting to build a model of a physical scene. The user identifies meaningful points, edges, planes, or object classes, and the system estimates the remaining geometry from images or measurements.

Human input resolves semantic or ambiguous choices that full automation may miss, while optimization reduces repetitive precision work. The physical object remains visible for immediate comparison with the reconstructed result.

3847.title: Semantic Knowledge
3847.heading: Semantic Knowledge
3847.content:
Semantic knowledge describes what tracked physical and virtual entities mean and how they relate, beyond their geometric shape and pose. An AR object may be identified as a machine component, destination, control, person, or task step with associated properties and actions.

This knowledge lets the system select relevant information, enforce interaction rules, and attach authored content to meaningful referents. Geometry answers where an entity is; semantics helps determine what the application should do with it.

3850.title: Semantic Distance
3850.heading: Semantic Distance
3850.content:
Semantic distance is the gap between feedback presented by a system and the meaning a player must derive from it. Clear, contextual signals shorten this distance; obscure or indirect signals make the player spend more effort interpreting state.

Reducing semantic distance helps [[Feedback]] update the [[Player Mental Model]] quickly. Together with low [[Articulatory Distance]], it keeps the interactive loop focused on the game rather than on operating the interface.

3853.content:
The book uses two complementary views of narrative semantics. A Euclidean factor map expresses the web of relationships among scenes and words; a hierarchy over their sequence can mark novelty, anomaly, or a major turn in that web.

In its Casablanca example, adjacent scenes that merge only high in the sequence-constrained tree signal stronger change than scenes joined low down. The same principle applies to sub-scenes or tweets. A breakpoint is an analytical indication for interpretation, not proof that one unique human reading is correct.

3874.title: Self-Inductance
3874.heading: Self-Inductance

An inductor stores magnetic energy $U=\tfrac12LI^2$, so abrupt current change requires a correspondingly large voltage.

3892.title: Selective Availability
3892.heading: Selective Availability
3892.content: Selective Availability was the intentional degradation of open GPS accuracy to preserve a military advantage while still supporting civilian navigation. It altered broadcast clock or orbital information so unauthorized receivers obtained a noisier solution. Differential correction largely defeated its practical effect, and policy shifted repeatedly before President Bill Clinton ordered it set permanently to zero in 2000. The episode shows that navigation accuracy can be governed as access, not only engineered as performance.

3895.title: Selection Sort
3895.heading: Selection Sort
3895.content:
Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum item in the unsorted portion of a collection and swaps it into the next final position. Each pass expands the sorted prefix by one item.

For $n$ items, repeated minimum searches give $O(n^2)$ [[Time Complexity]]. The method is easy to understand and implement, but faster loglinear algorithms are preferred when the collection is large.

3898.heading: Selection Control Structure
3898.content:
A selection control structure evaluates a condition and chooses which alternative sequence of steps to execute. It lets an [[Algorithm]] respond differently to different states or input values.

In Euclid's algorithm, testing whether the remainder is zero selects between stopping with the greatest common divisor and continuing the calculation. Selection can be nested inside an [[Iteration Control Structure]] so the decision is reconsidered after each repetition.

Seeded semi-supervised clustering begins with a small set of labeled or trusted example points for some groups. Seeds initialize representatives or influence assignments while unlabeled observations provide the remaining structure.

Seeds can align clusters with known categories using far less labeling than supervised classification. Incorrect, unrepresentative, or uneven seeds can steer the entire partition, so sensitivity to seed choice should be tested.

3907.title: Segment Cast
3907.heading: Segment Cast
3907.content:
A segment cast tests one [[Line Segment Geometry|line segment]] against registered collision objects and reports the nearest valid hit. A hit record can contain the object, intersection point, surface normal, and segment parameter.

The finite range distinguishes it from an unbounded ray cast and suits projectiles or movement over one update. Selecting the smallest nonnegative parameter ensures nearer geometry blocks objects behind it.

3910.title: Seebeck Effect
3910.heading: Seebeck Effect
3910.content: The Seebeck effect produces an electrical potential when a conductor has a temperature gradient, even before current flows. In a pair of different materials, the difference between their responses gives a voltage across hot and cold junctions. That voltage is the direct heat-to-electricity basis of a [[Thermoelectric Generator]]; it is not heat released by current through resistance.

3913.heading: Security Sandboxing
3913.content:
Security sandboxing runs code inside a restricted container whose access to files, memory, devices, and other resources is deliberately limited. Potentially harmful behavior can be observed or contained without granting the code ordinary host permissions.

Quarantined files are one application of this separation model. A sandbox reduces impact but still depends on the correctness of the boundary that mediates every attempted escape or resource request.

3916.title: Seebeck Coefficient
3916.heading: Seebeck Coefficient
3916.content: The Seebeck coefficient relates a material's induced potential gradient to its imposed temperature gradient, with units of volts per kelvin. For a p-type and n-type pair, their differential coefficient determines the junction voltage across a temperature range. The source notes opposite signs for the two types, helping their useful voltages add. See [[Seebeck Effect]] and [[Thermoelectric Figure of Merit]].

3922.title: Security Risk
3922.heading: Security Risk
3922.content:
Security risk expresses the likelihood and consequence of a security breach in relation to a threat and the system's vulnerability to it. The book presents a simple quantitative view in which risk grows as either threat level or vulnerability level grows.

A risk assessment helps prioritize controls rather than treating every possible event as equally urgent. The assessment must follow the data, users, systems, and providers across the complete cloud service boundary.

The source expresses a qualitative cyber-risk relationship as threat multiplied by vulnerability and impact. The values depend on context and expert judgment, but the structure forces an assessment to connect an exploitable weakness and potential actor with consequences for a particular asset.

This immune-inspired property can accelerate recognition and response, but stored experience must be updated when attackers change techniques. It complements both [[Signature-Based Threat Detection]] and a changing [[Behavioral Security Baseline]].

3928.content:
Security event monitoring collects and analyzes records from firewalls, identity systems, servers, applications, and protective tools. Because these logs grow too quickly for continuous manual review, software filters them for patterns that warrant an alert.

Useful monitoring connects an event to a user, service, action, and data boundary. Alerts need a common format and a timely response path so evidence can lead to investigation or remediation instead of remaining unread.

A security information and event management system brings evidence together from network devices, hosts, and applications. This cross-layer view is especially useful when an attack leaves partial traces at every level of [[Defense in Depth]] rather than one decisive event in a single log.

3931.heading: Security Container
3931.content:
A security container is a boundary around users, systems, software, storage, backups, and other elements that share the same security requirements. Components inside the boundary are permitted to trust one another according to the container's policy.

Network segmentation and virtual networks can isolate one container from another, while firewalls control crossings. Identification, [[Authentication]], and [[Authorization]] then determine who may enter and what an accepted user may do.

3937.title: Security Breach
3937.heading: Security Breach
3937.content:
A security breach is an event in which information or a computer system is used, accessed, changed, controlled, or made unavailable outside its intended rules. Different breaches can violate confidentiality, possession, integrity, authenticity, availability, or utility.

Describing which property failed helps identify the appropriate response. Unauthorized reading calls for different evidence and remediation than altered records, service denial, false origin, or loss of the only usable copy.

3949.content:
The Secure Shell protocol provides encrypted remote login, command execution, tunneling, and subsystem channels over a network connection. Its architecture separates secure transport, user authentication, and the multiplexed connection layer.

The transport tier authenticates the server and protects message integrity, the authentication tier validates the client, and the connection tier carries distinct interactive or forwarded channels within the secured session.

3952.heading: Secure Origin
3952.content:
A secure origin is a web origin delivered through HTTPS without active mixed content. The encrypted and authenticated connection prevents network intermediaries from silently changing the code delivered to the browser.

Browsers require this trust boundary before enabling sensitive capabilities such as a [[Service Worker]]. Local development may receive a special exception, but a deployed progressive web application needs HTTPS.

3958.content:
Sectoral information regulation applies different rules to information practices in fields such as government, defense, commerce, industry, and science. Each sector has distinct purposes, powers, evidence needs, and consequences for affected people.

A sectoral approach helps identify specialized duties, but it can fragment oversight when the same data move between institutions. Analysis must therefore follow both the original setting and later transfers or combinations.

3961.title: Secretary Problem
3961.heading: Secretary Problem
3961.content:
The secretary problem is an [[Optimal Stopping Problem]] in which candidates arrive one at a time, must be accepted or rejected immediately, and cannot be revisited. The objective is to maximize the probability of choosing the best candidate.

For $n$ randomly ordered candidates, the strategy first observes and rejects roughly the initial $n/e$, using their best member as a benchmark. It then selects the first later candidate better than that benchmark. The method succeeds in about $1/e$, or 37 percent, of cases, and no competing rule has a higher probability under these assumptions.

Second-order design specifies the tokens, rules, state space, and systems from which play emerges rather than scripting one exact path through the experience. The designer directly creates conditions and indirectly shapes the player's journey.

Its success depends on whether the resulting [[Play Space]] offers multiple viable paths and [[Meaningful Decision|meaningful decisions]]. The designer evaluates those indirect results through iterative prototyping, [[Playtesting]], and the [[Designer Loop]].

3967.content: The second law of thermodynamics gives a preferred direction to macroscopic change. Heat does not spontaneously flow from colder to hotter bodies, and no cyclic engine can convert all absorbed heat into work. Equivalently, the total [[Entropy]] of an isolated system does not decrease, explaining why many energy-conserving processes are irreversible.

3970.title: Searched Variable
3970.heading: Searched Variable
3970.content:
A searched variable is a variable whose conditional probability distribution is requested by a Bayesian question. At least one searched variable is required because it defines what the inference is trying to determine.

The answer retains the searched variable's alternatives and normalizes probability across them for the instantiated evidence. A variable can be searched in one question and known or free in another.

3973.title: Search-Based Feature Selection
3973.heading: Search-Based Feature Selection
3973.content:
Search-based feature selection treats a candidate subset as a point in a combinatorial space and explores that space for a good evaluation score. Complete, sequential, and randomized strategies trade optimality guarantees against feasible runtime.

The evaluator may be independent of a predictor or tied to one. Because the number of subsets grows exponentially, practical search relies on heuristics, pruning, stopping rules, or sparse optimization.

3976.title: Search Space
3976.heading: Search Space
3976.content:
A search space is the domain of possible values or candidates within which a [[Search Algorithm]] looks for a solution. Information gained during the search can remove portions that can no longer contain an acceptable answer.

In [[Binary Search]], comparing the target with the middle ordered item eliminates at least half of the current search space. The process repeats until a match is found or the space becomes empty.

3979.heading: Search Result Ranking
3979.content:
Search result ranking orders pages that match a query so the most useful candidates appear first. Content matching alone cannot distinguish authoritative pages from trivial or misleading pages when all contain the requested terms.

[[PageRank]] contributes a structural signal by treating links from other pages as endorsements whose weight depends on the importance of the source. A complete search engine may combine this signal with query content and other information.

3982.heading: Search Engine Index
3982.content:
A search engine index is the stored representation of web-page content gathered by a [[Web Crawler]]. It allows a search engine to find documents matching a query without rereading the live web for every request.

Matching is only one part of search. A common query may retrieve enormous numbers of pages, so [[Search Result Ranking]] must order the candidates to place likely relevant and authoritative results first.

3985.title: Search Algorithm
3985.heading: Search Algorithm
3985.content:
A search algorithm locates a target within a collection or determines that no acceptable target is present. The available structure determines what strategy is possible: an unordered collection may require [[Linear Search]], while ordered data enables [[Binary Search]].

Search problems also differ in what counts as success. Exact search requires a match, [[Approximate Search]] accepts sufficiently similar items, and an [[Optimal Stopping Problem]] requires a choice before later candidates are known.

An SDK-style Windows desktop project uses the compact `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop` project format to build Windows Forms or WPF software on .NET Core 3. Properties select the executable type, target framework, language version, and the desktop UI framework used by the project.

Package and project references are declared explicitly in the project file, which makes the build inputs easier to inspect than older verbose formats. 3991.title: Scrumban
3991.heading: Scrumban
3991.content:
Scrumban combines Scrum's goal-oriented Sprint cadence with Kanban's visualization and work-in-progress controls. A team can reserve a board area for Sprint work while using flow policies for production, support, or other continuously arriving items.

The combination is useful when exploratory feature work and predictable content flow coexist. Its practices should solve observed coordination problems rather than accumulate as process decoration.

3994.title: Scrum
3994.heading: Scrum
3994.content:
Scrum is an empirical framework in which a small [[Scrum Team]] creates a usable [[Product Increment]] during a fixed [[Sprint]]. Its roles, events, and artifacts make the state of the product and the way of working visible enough to inspect and adapt.

Scrum does not prescribe the engineering or creative techniques used inside a Sprint. It creates a cadence and accountabilities within which a team can discover and improve those techniques.

3997.title: Scrum Values
3997.heading: Scrum Values
3997.content:
The Scrum values are focus, courage, openness, commitment, and respect. Focus directs attention to the current goal; courage permits difficult work and conversations; openness exposes progress and problems; commitment supports shared goals; respect recognizes each contributor's capability.

The framework's events cannot create empiricism by themselves. These values make honest inspection, collaborative decisions, and meaningful adaptation possible.

4000.title: Scrum Team
4000.heading: Scrum Team
4000.content:
A Scrum Team combines a [[Product Owner]], [[Scrum Master]], and [[Development Team]] around one product goal. The roles divide accountability for value, process improvement, and delivery without dividing ownership of the outcome.

In game development, the team is cross-discipline so that playable value can move from idea through implementation, art, audio, design, and testing inside the same Sprint.

4003.title: Scrum Principles
4003.heading: Scrum Principles
4003.content:
Scrum is organized around empiricism, emergence, collaboration, [[Timebox|timeboxing]], prioritization, and self-organization. Together these principles let a team make decisions from observable results while keeping work bounded and directed toward value.

They explain why Scrum practices are structured as they are: a working increment enables inspection, an ordered backlog focuses effort, and a self-managing team adapts the implementation as knowledge emerges.

4005.sourceSearchName: scrum of scrums scrum of scrums
4005.title: Scrum of Scrums
4005.heading: Document

4006.sourceSearchName: scrum of scrums scrum of scrums
4006.title: Scrum of Scrums
4006.heading: Scrum of Scrums
4006.content:
A Scrum of Scrums is a cross-team coordination event focused on dependencies, integration, and obstacles that affect more than one team. Representatives bring information and decisions back to their teams rather than reporting upward for individual control.

The event should resolve or route cross-team problems. Repeating each team's ordinary status creates meeting overhead without improving the whole game.

4007.sourceSearchName: scrum of scrums scrum of scrums
4007.title: Scrum of Scrums
4007.heading: References

4009.title: Scrum Master
4009.heading: Scrum Master
4009.content:
A Scrum Master helps a team use and improve Scrum. The role coaches self-management, facilitates events, exposes impediments, protects the team from disruptive interference, and helps the wider organization create conditions for effective work.

The Scrum Master does not assign the team's tasks or act as its status collector. Authority comes from service, facilitation, and improving the system in which the team operates.

4012.title: Scrolling Background
4012.heading: Scrolling Background
4012.content:
A scrolling background presents a game world larger than the display by moving the visible region as the player travels. Single-direction scrolling can recycle background segments after they leave the view, while bidirectional movement must retain or regenerate segments that may reappear.

The camera should begin moving only when the controlled object reaches the intended screen threshold. Separating world position from screen position keeps the world coherent while the viewport changes.

The engine can pause, resume, or invoke scripted behavior through this controlled runtime. Interpretation adds overhead, but the virtual machine provides portability and a clear boundary between scripts and lower-level engine code.

A screen-space lighting pass reads surface properties from a [[G-Buffer]] and calculates illumination for the pixels covered by a light. Global lights can use a full-screen shape, while a point light can render geometry approximating its region of influence.

Additive blending accumulates contributions from multiple lights. Depth and stencil techniques can limit work and address cases where light volumes cross surfaces or contain the camera.

4021.title: Screen Tearing
4021.heading: Screen Tearing
4021.content:
Screen tearing occurs when the displayed image contains portions of different rendered frames. It happens when the front and back buffers are exchanged while the display is partway through scanning a frame.

Synchronizing the swap with the [[Vertical Blank Interval]] prevents the buffer change from becoming visible in the middle of the image. [[Double Buffering]] supplies the complete alternate frame that is presented at that safe point.

4024.title: Screen Space
4024.heading: Screen Space
4024.content:
Screen space is the two-dimensional coordinate system of the rendered viewport. The graphics pipeline maps projected geometry into pixel positions while retaining depth information for visibility testing.

Screen coordinates are useful for interface alignment and selection, but they no longer directly express the original three-dimensional position. [[Unprojection]] reverses part of the pipeline when a screen point must define a world-space ray.

Because it focuses on relationships rather than visual finish, it can guide an [[Game Interface Prototype|interface prototype]] before detailed assets exist. Each node should have a purpose in the player's larger path.

4036.title: Scope Creep
4036.heading: Scope Creep
4036.content:
Scope creep is the gradual addition of features, systems, or content after a project has established what it intends to build. Each apparently small addition carries implementation, integration, testing, balance, schedule, and risk costs.

A proposed addition should be evaluated against the [[Game Concept]], resources, and remaining time as if it were a small concept-stage project. Strong ideas that do not fit the current release can be preserved without burdening the existing [[Game Scope]].

An ordered [[Product Backlog]] makes this trade-off explicit: new value can enter, but the Product Owner reorders it against existing scope rather than quietly adding it to a fixed date. A [[Minimum Viable Game]] protects the release's essential value while lower-value additions remain negotiable.

4042.title: Scientific Notation
4042.heading: Scientific Notation
4042.content: Scientific notation writes a nonzero decimal as $a\times10^n$, where $1\leq |a|<10$ and $n$ is an integer. The exponent records how far the decimal point moves. Multiplication combines coefficients and adds exponents, making the notation especially useful for quantities that are much larger or smaller than ordinary decimal displays handle clearly.

4045.title: Schrodinger Equation
4045.heading: Schrodinger Equation
4045.content:
The Schrodinger equation governs the evolution of a nonrelativistic quantum state. In one dimension its time-dependent form is

$$i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}+V\right)\psi.$$

The wavefunction itself is not a material wave; $|\psi|^2$ supplies a probability density for measurement outcomes.

4060.title: Scene Purpose
4060.heading: Scene Purpose
4060.content:
Scene purpose is the specific idea, rule, relationship, or feeling that a [[Game Scene]] is constructed to develop. A designer should be able to state what the scene contributes and how established game vocabulary produces that contribution.

Purpose keeps a scene from becoming unrelated spectacle or clutter. Tension, timing, discovery, or a strategic insight should arise from [[Game Rule|rules]] and objects the player can understand, so the experience continues the game's existing conversation.

4063.title: Scene Iteration
4063.heading: Scene Iteration
4063.content:
Scene iteration is the repeated cycle of constructing a [[Game Scene]], playing it, identifying problems, and revising its arrangement. Each draft tests whether the scene communicates its purpose and supports the intended choices.

Iteration treats a first layout as a hypothesis rather than a finished answer. Changes should solve observed problems while preserving the established rules and relationships that make the scene intelligible.

4066.title: Scene Shape
4066.heading: Scene Shape
4066.content:
Scene shape is the overall arrangement of choices and constraints within a [[Game Scene]]. It describes how the available paths widen, narrow, branch, and converge without requiring the designer to predict every exact action.

Alternating broad choice with focused demands creates [[Game Pacing|pacing]]. A scene can guide play toward a particular point while preserving [[Player Performance|individual performance]], much as walls define a room without determining every movement inside it.

4069.title: Scene Graph
4069.heading: Scene Graph
4069.content:
A scene graph is a hierarchical representation of objects and transformations in a spatial scene. A child inherits the coordinate transformation of its parent, allowing assemblies and attached augmentations to move through changes applied higher in the hierarchy.

AR scene graphs can represent both physical and virtual objects and connect them to tracked frames. Rendering traverses the graph, while application behavior may use the same structure for visibility, grouping, and interaction.

4072.title: Scalar
4072.heading: Scalar
4072.content:
A scalar is a single numerical value, distinguished from a [[Vector]] or [[Matrix]]. In a linear combination, scalars multiply vectors or matrix columns and determine the contribution of each component.

Linear-model coefficients are scalars collected into a coefficient vector. Their numerical values are unknown parameters or estimates, while the predictor columns they weight are treated as known quantities in the design.

4075.title: Scene Composition
4075.heading: Scene Composition
4075.content:
Scene composition is the visual arrangement of elements that directs attention and gives a playable space a particular character. Framing, contrast, repetition, symmetry, and directional shapes can show what matters before the player understands every rule.

Composition can also convey mood or function: symmetry may suggest an artificial structure, irregularity a natural landscape, and an open view a pause from danger. Its visual guidance should support the [[Scene Purpose]].

4078.title: Scatter Plot
4078.heading: Scatter Plot
4078.content:
A scatter plot places paired measurements as points on two quantitative axes. It can reveal direction, curvature, clusters, changing variance, and unusual observations before a correlation or regression coefficient is interpreted.

Color or symbol can encode a grouping variable so analysts can see whether the overall pattern differs across subpopulations. Heavy overplotting, restricted ranges, and influential outliers can all obscure the relationship and should be considered when styling the graph.

In the source's paired-height example, plotting every father-son observation reveals a relationship that the two marginal means and standard deviations omit. The graph provides the context needed to interpret a [[Pearson Correlation Coefficient]] rather than treating the coefficient as a complete description.

The book implements scatter plots in an R grammar-of-graphics workflow, mapping variables to axes and optional color groups. Faceting, labels, and explicit export settings turn the exploratory display into a reproducible analytic artifact.

4081.content:
Scaled partial pivoting compares potential pivots relative to the largest magnitude entry in each candidate row. It chooses the row with the largest ratio rather than the largest raw entry.

This protects [[Gaussian Elimination]] when rows have very different scales, because a moderately sized pivot may still be dangerously small compared with the other coefficients in its row.

4084.title: Scalar Triple Product
4084.heading: Scalar Triple Product
4084.content: The scalar triple product is $u\cdot(v\times w)$. Its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors, and its sign records orientation. Cyclic permutations preserve the value, while interchanging two vectors reverses the sign. A zero value means the vectors are coplanar.

4087.title: Scalar Multiplication of a Matrix
4087.heading: Scalar Multiplication of a Matrix
4087.content:
Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry of a [[Matrix]] by the same number. For $A=(a_{ij})$ and scalar $k$, the matrix $kA$ has entries $ka_{ij}$ and keeps the dimensions of $A$.

It distributes over [[Matrix Addition]] and over addition of scalars. Multiplication by zero produces the [[Zero Matrix]], while multiplication by $-1$ produces the additive inverse of the matrix.

Finite element characteristic matrices often appear as a geometric matrix multiplied by a scalar material-and-size factor, such as axial rigidity divided by element length. Scalar multiplication preserves the matrix pattern while changing its physical scale.

4090.title: Scalar Multiplication of a Vector
4090.heading: Scalar Multiplication of a Vector
4090.content:
Scalar multiplication multiplies every component of a vector by the same scalar. It changes magnitude and may reverse direction while preserving the vector's line.

Together with [[Vector Addition]], it must satisfy the vector-space distributive and associative axioms. Weighted sums formed from these operations are [[Linear Combination|linear combinations]].

4093.title: Scalar Matrix
4093.heading: Scalar Matrix
4093.content:
A scalar matrix is a [[Diagonal Matrix]] whose diagonal entries are all the same scalar. It has the form $cI$, where $I$ is the [[Identity Matrix]].

Scalar matrices commute with every compatible square matrix. The special cases $c=1$ and $c=0$ produce the identity and zero matrices.

4096.title: Scalar Extension for Modules
4096.heading: Scalar Extension for Modules
4096.content:
Given a ring homomorphism R → S and an R-module M, extension of scalars forms the S-module S ⊗_R M. The factor S supplies the new scalar action.

If M is finitely generated over R, its scalar extension is finitely generated over S. [[Localization of a Module]] is the special case obtained by extending scalars to a localized ring.
